title: Huawei convicted by US jury of stealing trade secrets and bank fraud in eight-year Iran case
summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn found Huawei and three subsidiaries guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets, while acquitting the company of racketeering. Sentencing is set for September 14, 2027.
content:
A federal jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday convicted Huawei Technologies and three of its subsidiaries of bank fraud, wire fraud, violating United States sanctions on Iran and conspiring to steal trade secrets from American companies, delivering a verdict in a criminal case that has shaped the rivalry between Washington and Beijing over technology for eight years.

The jury found the Chinese telecommunications giant guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced, according to [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/chinas-huawei-convicted-us-criminal-trial-stemming-iran-business-2026-11-24/). The verdict followed a trial of more than two months in the Eastern District of New York, in which prosecutors called more than 60 witnesses and the defence called 15. Jurors deliberated for four days before returning their decision.

Huawei was acquitted on the two counts prosecutors had presented as the most serious: conspiring to run a racketeering enterprise and conspiring to obstruct justice. The acquittal on the racketeering charge, which had accused the company of acting as a criminal enterprise, was the clearest win for the defence in a case the government had framed as a two-decade conspiracy to dominate the global telecoms market. Huawei's lead lawyer told reporters afterwards that he had "profoundly mixed emotions" about the verdict, noting that the racketeering count had been the single lead charge brought by the United States.

At the centre of the case was Huawei's business in Iran. Prosecutors told the jury that the company conducted operations in Iran through its subsidiary Skycom while misleading major global banks, including HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas, into believing Skycom was an independent business partner. The deception, they argued, allowed Huawei to obtain billions of dollars in financing and to keep access to US dollar-clearing services while evading American sanctions. "For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," the US Justice Department said in a statement after the verdict.

The trade secrets counts covered some of the most detailed allegations aired during the trial. Prosecutors said Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its internet routers, took antenna technology from the wireless company Quintel, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by the semiconductor company CNEX. In one episode described in court, Huawei employees gained access to a T-Mobile testing laboratory and stole technical data about the carrier's robot, known as Tappy, which tests touchscreen responsiveness. Engineers photographed the robot and carried off one of its parts in a backpack, prosecutors said. The employee involved was later dismissed, defence lawyers told the court.

The three subsidiaries convicted alongside the parent company are Huawei Device Co Ltd, Futurewei Technologies Inc and Huawei Device USA Inc. Sentencing has been scheduled for September 14, 2027, before US District Judge Ann Donnelly, when the defendants face criminal fines, forfeiture and restitution. The long gap before sentencing means the financial consequences of the verdict will not be known for almost ten months.

The case began in 2018 and surfaced publicly that December, when Huawei's chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, the daughter of the company's founder, was arrested in Canada on a US warrant. The following year, Washington placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to American technology, citing national security concerns. The company, which had grown into one of the world's biggest suppliers of equipment for wireless telecommunications networks, has been at the centre of US-China competition ever since, with American technology companies long accusing it of stealing their business secrets.

For all its significance, the verdict changes little about Huawei's position in the United States in the short term. The company remains on the US Entity List, the blacklist imposed in 2019, and it is already largely shut out of the American market. What the conviction does is put a judicial stamp on the government's longstanding claims, and it gives prosecutors a formal finding that Huawei's rise was built in part on fraud and theft. That finding is likely to harden the political case in Washington for keeping restrictions in place, even as the two governments continue to negotiate over trade.

The timing underlines how central technology has become to the US-China relationship. The verdict arrived in the same week that Washington moved to impose new tariffs on China and other trading partners over industrial subsidies, and days after the leaders of the United States, China and Russia met in Shenzhen. Read more about that summit in our report on the [Xi-Trump-Putin meeting in Shenzhen](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19). The technology rivalry is also playing out on other fronts, including the investigation into chipmaker Nvidia's accounting that sent its shares plunging this week, covered in our report on the [SEC probe into Nvidia](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/sec-probes-nvidia-accounting-shares-plunge-november-2026).

For now, the case that began with an arrest in Vancouver eight years ago has ended with a guilty verdict in Brooklyn, and with the company's reputation in the United States formally defined by a jury.
